name: The John Brunt V.C.
text: Your train passes the John Brunt V.C. pub in Paddock Wood, on the train's {side}. Once the Kent Arms, it was renamed in 1947 after John Brunt, who spent his teenage years in the town and won the Victoria Cross in the Second World War.

name: Somerhill House
text: Your train passes near Somerhill House, on the train's {side}, a Jacobean mansion built from 1611 to 1613 for the Earl of Clanricarde. Turner painted it in 1811, and it is now a school.

name: St Michael and All Angels Church, Marden
text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church, Marden, on the train's {side}, built at the end of the 12th century. The church is the picture on the village sign.

name: Marden Meadows
text: Your train passes Marden Meadows, on the train's {side}, three fields of unimproved grassland that are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. They are mown for hay once a year, and green-winged orchids grow there.

name: St Peter and St Paul's Church, Headcorn
text: Your train passes near Headcorn's parish church, on the train's {side}. By its south door are the remains of the Headcorn Oak, said to be up to 1,200 years old, though one expert reckoned it nearer 500.

name: Headcorn Aerodrome
text: Your train passes near Headcorn Aerodrome, on the train's {side}, a grass airfield that opened in 1943 as RAF Lashenden, a name chosen to confuse the enemy. Today it is home to Kent's only skydiving club.

name: Godinton Park
text: Your train runs beside Godinton Park, on the train's {side}. Its Jacobean house was home to the Toke family for about 455 years, and its garden has one of the longest yew hedges in England.

name: Archbishop's Palace, Charing
text: Your train passes near the Archbishop's Palace at Charing, on the train's {side}, one of the earliest properties of the archbishops of Canterbury. In 1520 Henry VIII stayed here with an entourage of more than 5,000 on his way to the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

name: St Mary's Church, Lenham
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, Lenham, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 14th century after a fire destroyed the one before. It and the nearby tithe barn are both Grade I listed.

name: Bell Farm House
text: Your train passes near Bell Farm House in Harrietsham, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed farmhouse built around 1500. Its hall wall is still blackened by smoke from the days before it had a chimney.

name: Leeds Castle
text: Your train passes within a kilometre of the parkland of Leeds Castle, on the train's {side}. The castle stands on islands in a lake made by the River Len; Henry VIII used it as a home for his first wife, Catherine of Aragon.

name: Holy Cross Church, Bearsted
text: Your train passes near Holy Cross Church, Bearsted, on the train's {side}, begun in the 13th century. Three stone beasts sit on the corners of its tower, replacing worn originals that may have shown wolves from a family coat of arms.

name: Mote Park
text: Your train passes near Mote Park, on the train's {side}, a public park of about 450 acres in Maidstone. Its name comes from an Old English word for a place of assembly, and it has a boating lake and a miniature railway.

name: Maidstone Museum
text: Your train passes near Maidstone Museum, on the train's {side}, built round Chillington Manor, an Elizabethan house finished in 1577. It opened in 1858 with the collections of a local doctor, and has one of the most important Japanese collections outside London.

name: East Malling Research Station
text: Your train passes near the fruit research station at East Malling, on the train's {side}, set up in 1913. Its research, above all on rootstocks for fruit trees, earned it a worldwide reputation.

name: St James the Great's Church, East Malling
text: Your train passes near St James the Great's Church, East Malling, on the train's {side}, with a nave of the 14th century. Sir Thomas Twisden lies here, a judge at the trials of the regicides of Charles I.

name: Malling Abbey
text: Your train passes near Malling Abbey in West Malling, on the train's {side}, founded for Benedictine nuns around 1090 by Gundulf, Bishop of Rochester. It was dissolved in 1538, became a monastery again in the late 19th century, and is now home to Anglican Benedictine nuns.

name: Oldbury Hill
text: Your train passes near the Iron Age hillfort on Oldbury Hill, on the train's {side}, thought to have been built around 100 BC. At 123 acres it was the largest of a line of forts across Kent and Surrey, and flint tools from the Palaeolithic have been found there too.

name: Greatness Brickworks
text: Your train passes near Greatness Brickworks, on the train's {side}, a Site of Special Scientific Interest in Sevenoaks for its Cretaceous rocks, which are rich in fossils, above all ammonites. It is private land.

name: Newtown, Ashford
text: Your train passes Newtown, on the train's {side}, built by the South Eastern Railway from 1847 for the workers at its Ashford works. It was first called Alfred Town, and was laid out round a green.

name: Royal Military Canal
text: Your train crosses the Royal Military Canal, dug from 1804 along the edge of Romney Marsh as a barrier against Napoleon's planned invasion. Early in the Second World War it was fortified again, and many of its pillboxes survive.

name: The Landgate, Rye
text: Your train passes near the Landgate at Rye, on the train's {side}, the only one left of the town's four fortified gateways, dating from 1329. In 2015 some 25 tonnes of pigeon droppings had to be cleared from its arch.

name: Ypres Tower
text: Your train passes near Ypres Tower in Rye, on the train's {side}, built in the 13th or 14th century to defend the town and once called Baddings Tower. It was later a prison, and is now part of Rye Castle Museum.

name: Winchelsea
text: Your train passes near Winchelsea, on the train's {side}, a town planned on a grid on higher ground after storms ravaged the old town on the shingle. Edward I granted it a charter in 1281.

name: Doleham station
text: Doleham station, at one end of this stretch, is a single-platform halt that opened as Guestling Halt in 1907. It serves only a handful of houses, and before the pandemic about eight people a day used it.

name: Speckled Wood
text: Your train passes near Speckled Wood, on the train's {side}, a steep-sided, wet woodland park in Ore. It is thought to take its name from the speckled wood butterflies that thrive there.

name: Hastings Castle
text: Your train passes near Hastings Castle, on the train's {side}, begun in 1066 on William of Normandy's orders, before the Battle of Hastings. It stands on the West Hill cliffs, and large parts of it have fallen into the sea.

name: Hastings Museum and Art Gallery
text: Your train passes near Hastings Museum and Art Gallery, on the train's {side}, founded in 1892. Its Durbar Hall was part of an Indian palace built for the Indian and Colonial Exhibition of 1886.

name: Marine Court
text: Your train passes near Marine Court on the seafront at St Leonards, on the train's {side}, a block of flats built from 1936 to 1938 to look like the liner Queen Mary. Its curved eastern end steps back as it rises, like the forecastle of a ship.

name: Wye College
text: Your train passes near Wye College, on the train's {side}, founded in 1447 by Cardinal John Kempe as a chantry college that taught local children. It later became an agricultural college of the University of London, and closed in 2009.

name: Westenhanger Castle
text: Your train passes Westenhanger Castle, on the train's {side}, a fortified manor house of the 14th century. In 1588 Elizabeth I used it as the headquarters for Kent's 14,000 troops against the Spanish Armada.

name: Folkestone Racecourse
text: Your train passes near Folkestone Racecourse at Westenhanger, on the train's {side}, where racing began in 1898. It closed in 2012, and its grandstand can be seen from the station.

name: Saltwood Castle
text: Your train passes near Saltwood Castle, on the train's {side}, which belonged to the archbishops of Canterbury until 1540. In 1953 the art historian Kenneth Clark bought it, and his son, the diarist Alan Clark, lived there later.

name: Cheriton Road
text: Your train passes near the Cheriton Road sports grounds in Folkestone, on the train's {side}, home of Folkestone Invicta. Cricket has been played there since 1901, and Kent County Cricket Club has used the ground.

name: Samphire Hoe
text: Your train passes Samphire Hoe, on the train's {side}, a country park at the foot of the White Cliffs made from 4.9 million cubic metres of chalk dug out for the Channel Tunnel. It opened in 1997 and is named after rock samphire, which Shakespeare mentions in King Lear.

name: Dover Priory
text: Your train passes the remains of Dover Priory, on the train's {side}; the railway was built across the western part of its site. Dover College uses its old buildings, and the 12th-century Strangers' Refectory is still in use.

name: Lydden and Temple Ewell Downs
text: Your train passes Lydden and Temple Ewell Downs, on the train's {side}, some of the richest chalk downland in Kent, with adonis blues and silver-spotted skippers. In June 2025 the Dover twist moth was found here, not seen in England since 1952.

name: Shepherdswell (East Kent Railway)
text: Your train passes the East Kent Railway's station at Shepherdswell, on the train's {side}. It opened in 1916 as the end of the East Kent Light Railway, closed to passengers in 1948, and reopened as a heritage line in 1993.

name: Snowdown
text: Your train passes near Snowdown, on the train's {side}, a hamlet that was home to one of the four chief collieries of the Kent coalfield. The colliery closed in 1987.

name: Aylesham
text: Your train passes near Aylesham, on the train's {side}, a village begun in 1926 for miners at the newly sunk Snowdown Colliery. Its planner, Sir Patrick Abercrombie, meant it to grow into a town of up to 30,000 people.
